title: Al-Bari', the Maker
hookLine: the Maker, who brings forth from nothing, without flaw
tomorrow: if He shapes every face, can Amira paint one on the wall?

lines: THE PLAN, THE BUILD, THE FINISH.
cards: Home makeover shows run on three people: the designer with the plan, the crew who builds it, and the one who picks the tile and the lights at the end. Nobody mixes them up. So, yesterday's question.
Near the end of surah fifty-nine, Pickthall's translation reads: "He is Allah, the Creator, the Shaper out of naught, the Fashioner." Creator, Shaper, Fashioner. Three making words in one breath.
Isn't that saying the same thing three times?

teach.h: THE PLAN, THE BUILD, THE FORM.
teach.b: Al-Ghazali asked the same question in his book on the names, and he answered it with a building. First someone settles the plan: how much wood, how many bricks, where each wall stands. That's al-Khaliq, yesterday's name.
Then someone actually raises it out of the ground, following the plan.

teach.h: AL-BARI': THE ONE WHO BRINGS FORTH.
teach.b: That's today's name, al-Bari', the Maker, the One who brings forth. Then someone gives it its finished form, and that's tomorrow's name.
In a human building, al-Ghazali says, three different people might do those three jobs. In his reading, all three belong to the One. So the verse isn't repeating itself.
It's walking through making, one step at a time.

And look at Pickthall's phrase for today's step: the Shaper out of naught. A human maker always starts with something already there: clay, flour, paint, a blank page. Here the bringing forth doesn't wait for materials.
And the Maker brings forth without flaw.
Surah sixty-seven says no fault can be seen in the creation of the Beneficent, and then sets a test: "then look again: Canst thou see any rifts?"
Look again. The verse invites a second look, not blind agreement.

So here's the thing to tell a friend tonight: the Qur'an names making in three steps, and the middle one, bringing something out of nothing, is the step no human hand can copy. Ours always start with something given.

how: Muslims recite the last verses of surah al-Hashr, where al-Khaliq, al-Bari' and al-Musawwir stand together, and teachers of the names often explain the three as one sequence of making.

o: the One who brings things forth out of nothing
the One who repairs whatever has been broken
the One who protects what has been finished

games.q: the building in three steps — tap the pairs.

s: Creator, Shaper and Fashioner in one verse are three words for the same thing
al-Ghazali reads them as three steps: plan, bring forth, give form.
surah sixty-seven invites a second look at creation for any rift
then look again: canst thou see any rifts?
al-Ghazali explains the three names with a building
a plan, a build, a finish: in a human house, maybe three people; in his reading, one Maker.

games.q: a friend reads surah fifty-nine and says, 'Creator, Shaper, Fashioner: that's just poetry repeating itself.' what's the puzzle's solve?
o: each word is a step: plan, bring forth, give form, and all three are His.
it's repetition for rhythm; the three words mean exactly the same.
they're three different makers who each did one part of the job.
games.why: al-Ghazali's building: in a human house three people might split the work. in his reading of the verse, one Maker does all three.

practice: With whatever is near, a sheet of paper, a napkin, a bit of string, make one small thing with your hands: a fold, a knot, a paper boat. Notice you needed the paper before you could begin.
For the rest of the sit, hold what you made in your palm and keep one thought with it: everything I make starts with something given.

wordCard.voice: Al-Bari': the Maker, the One who brings forth, in Pickthall's words the Shaper out of naught. The middle step, between the plan and the form.

orig.note: Arabic: the Maker, the One who brings forth. Pickthall renders it 'the Shaper out of naught'.

carryVoice: For the road: he brings forth, out of nothing, and our hands begin with what's given. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: He is Allah, the Creator, the Shaper out of naught, the Fashioner.
then look again: Canst thou see any rifts?

sources.ref: al-Ghazali, al-Maqsad al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna (the builder analogy for al-Khaliq, al-Bari', al-Musawwir)
